<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The PKGBUILD file defines a standard binary package for xerahs, a screen capture and sharing tool. It fetches prebuilt release binaries from the project's official GitHub repository (https://github.com/ShareX/XerahS) over HTTPS, using version-pinned URLs. The source array includes the application binary tarballs for x86_64 and aarch64, along with a desktop file and assets (logo, license), all pulled from the same trusted upstream. Checksums (sha256sums) are provided for all sources, ensuring integrity verification at build time.

The package installation routine is straightforward: it extracts the binary tarball into `/usr/lib/xerahs`, sets appropriate permissions, creates symlinks in `/usr/bin`, and installs metadata (license, desktop file, icon). All operations are confined to the package directory and follow standard Arch Linux packaging practices. Dependencies are clearly declared, including both core runtime libraries and optional components for extended functionality. There are no network operations, dynamic downloads, or execution of fetched code during installation or runtime.

No obfuscated commands, eval usage, or suspicious scripts are present. The package does not modify system files outside its scope, install hooks, or perform any actions beyond installing the upstream binaries and associated metadata. While the binaries are not built from source (as expected for a -bin package), the use of pinned releases with verified checksums aligns with AUR best practices. There is no evidence of data exfiltration, backdoors, or supply-chain tampering.
</details>

It declares typical fields such as `Name`, `Exec`, `Icon`, and `Categories`, which are normal for application launchers. The `Exec` line points to `/usr/bin/xerahs`, a standard system binary path, and uses the `%U` placeholder for URL arguments, which is appropriate for MIME handler declarations. There are no scripts, commands, or executable logic embedded in this file.

The file includes metadata like `MimeType=x-scheme-handler/xerahs`, indicating support for a custom URI scheme, which is common for applications that handle deep links or protocol-based activation. While URI handlers can theoretically be abused in supply-chain attacks, the presence alone is not malicious—it is a legitimate feature for inter-application communication. No evidence of obfuscated commands, network activity, or file system manipulation exists in this file.

Additionally, desktop entries may include environment-specific hints like `X-GNOME-UsesNotifications` or KDE D-Bus restrictions, which are benign and used for UI integration. The `StartupWMClass` ensures proper window grouping, and `Terminal=false` confirms it's a GUI application. All fields align with standard desktop entry specifications (freedesktop.org), and nothing suggests injected or malicious behavior.
</details>
